title: How did the old-school Hollywood filmmakers react to the French New Wave?

commenti.body:
This is an interesting question, and I'm afraid I don't have answers to provide.

I just pulled my copy of Hitchcock/Truffaut of the shelf (every home should have one) as I have not read it in a long time. For the most part it is Truffaut asking Hitch about his (Hitchcock's) films and Hitch proving a lot of interesting details. Hitch doesnt reference FNW films at all as far as I can tell from scanning the index, and Truffaut only brings them up as reference points in some of his supplementary writing.

I also did some index scans of some other Hitchcock, Ford, Huston and Welles biographies and came up with nothing as well. It might take searching through interviews in film magazines to come up with anything substantial.

Hitchcock/Truffaut is about Hitchcock's career. It has been a while since I read it but I do not recall there was much talk of Truffaut's movies in it.  It was meant as an introduction to Hitchcock for a new generation who did not know him much.  It is a fascinating read.

In Hitchcock's case, I believe he was deeply enthused by the European avant-garde of the 60s. In 1967, he was set to shoot a project called Kaleidoscope; he even sent the script to Truffaut. It seemed like it would be a more avant-garde and possibly violent film, influenced by Antonioni and Blow Up. However, the project was ultimately abandoned.
Hitch always liked pushing the envelope, he tried to go more wild with Frenzy.

I think Orson Welles liked it because he was always interested in trying new things but I know I heard him talk about some films in the 1970s being too dirty, he may have only been talking about Hollywood at that point.

From "This is Orson Welles" by Peter Bogdanovich:

Bogdanovich: I think we’d better have your thoughts on Godard.

Welles: Well, since you’re so very firm about it. He’s the definitive influence if not really the first film artist of this last decade, and his gifts as a director are enormous. I just can’t take him very seriously as a thinker—and that’s where we seem to differ, because he does. His message is what he cares about these days, and, like most movie messages, it could be written on the head of a pin. But what’s so admirable about him is his marvelous contempt for the machinery of movies and even movies themselves—a kind of anarchistic, nihilistic contempt for the medium—which, when he’s at his best and most vigorous, is very exciting.

David Lean admired them and was influences by them. That iconic cut in Lawrence of Arabia where a match turns into the sun was directly inspired by the experimental editing of the French New Wave.

Samuel Fuller and Fritz Lang respected them and took pride in being sort of fatherly figures to the moment, taking roles in films such as Pierrot le Fou and Contempt.

I have assumed that Hitchcock’s decision to cast Claude Jade in *Topaz* was due to at least Truffaut’s recommendation, if not seeing her in *Baisers voleés*. (I’m not sure if the shooting and release chronology lines up well enough for Hitchcock to have seen the Truffaut film.)
As a pretty big JLG fan I totally agree with this. Godard is at his best when he’s at his wackiest. Weekend and Pierrot Le Fou >>> Breathless, Vivre sa Vie, Masulin Feminin, Etc.
Yeah, and you can really tell he was inspired by other filmmakers with that movie. It felt more like a Giallo than a Hitchcock movie, and I actually liked that a lot.

I find it interesting that people always cut out most of the quote here, only having the part about the head of a pin. It's a much more even-handed take on Godard from Welles here than its usually presented as.

Welles even considered having Godard appear in Other Side of the Wind at one point!
I love Frenzy. It’s probably my favourite Hitchcock but no one really cares about it.
The story I heard is that he called The Last Picture Show a “dirty movie”. Which is bizarre, given that he went on to shoot The Other Side of the Wind not long after.
Pierrot and Weekend are highly philosophical movies

Yeah of course. I’m agreeing with the sentiment that he’s at his best when he’s vigorously anarchic and nihilistic. His black and white pictures are brooding. It doesn’t work as well as when he’s angry and contemptuous- for my sensibilities.

**John Huston** (reproduced in *Conversations with the Great Moviemakers of Hollywood's Golden Age*):

>*Earlier you spoke of your "school of filmmaking." Do you feel there is a tension between what you call your school and the best of what is being produced today?*  
I was speaking of the films that started in France, the Jean-Luc Godard films. I watched them with great interest. I'm a fan of Godard's work, but I couldn't make a film like that any more than a Quattrocento painter could do a Pollack. It's less true even than that. I have great admiration for the well-constructed screenplay, done from the inside out, from an idea, and where every line echoes that idea.  
*Where Godard would use a pan just to be artificial, you would probably use a cut to be natural. How do you feel about that sort of change in attitude toward technique within the last twenty years?*  
I think it's entirely a question of subject matter. I don't try to tell the stories that Godard tells. Assuming there is interest in his stories, then he goes about it the right way. Another picture that to some extent utilizes the so-called modern techniques is *Midnight Cowboy*, and I was lost in admiration for it. I thought it was simply a wonderful picture. It came to me as an experience, like the best of literature. I compare the character of Ratso with The Old Man and the Sea, for instance. He is a demonstration of human courage, almost exalted.

**Otto Preminger** (1961, talking to Eric Rohmer & Jacques Doniol-Valcroze):

>*Cahiers: And among the modern directors, where does your taste lie?*  
>  
>Preminger: I don't like to judge my colleagues.  
>  
>*Cahiers: Even the young ones?*  
>  
>Preminger: I have sympathies with the Nouvelle Vague-the French, at least, since I haven't seen Shadows and other New York films. The future belongs to them, no contest. One should not forget that making a cheap film is an advantage, inasmuch as the public and the critics are more inclined to forgive any clumsiness. Making one's first film is also an advantage. These two advantages don't present themselves again. One can't always shoot on a low budget, and the second time, one expects more from a film director, especially concerning the rigor of the story. I must say, too, that dramatic construction is not the strength of the Nouvelle Vague. Notwithstanding, I am in general quite partisan of all experimental films, since without experiment there is no progress.

**Otto Preminger** again (1966 or 1969, talking to Peter Bogdanovich):

>*Bogdanovich: When you first started making pictures, were there certain directors whose work influenced you?*  
>  
>Preminger: Nothing I do is that deliberate. Naturally, I am influenced by whatever I see, whether in life or on film or in the theatre. I try to see as many pictures as possible, good or bad, because I think it's necessary for anybody in any profession to keep abreast of the times.  
>  
>To give you an example, when the Nouvelle Vague came, they cut out all the opticals, all the dissolves and fades, not as an experiment but because they had no money. When I saw these films, I decided that dissolves slow up a film unless they are used with great discretion and not just automatically to denote a passage of time. So in my last films I haven't used them. In Hurry Sundown \[1966\], for instance, there isn't one dissolve-and only two fades, which are used because they work out nicely with the mood of the scene, not in the sense of a conventional "fade-out." In other words, I think that things should change, and when I see a deliberate experiment I like, I am influenced by it.

Yeah, almost every instance of this quote on the internet includes only the negative part. The full context makes it completely different. Welles appreciates exactly the aspects of Godard's filmmaking that I would have expected him to appreciate.
I think it was so unromantic about sex that it felt dirty to him.

Orson on Godard:  

"He's the definitive influence if not really the first film artist of this last decade [1960's] and his gifts as a director are enormous. I just can't take him very seriously as a thinker - and that's where we seem to differ because he does. His message is what he cares about these days, & like most movie messages, it could be written on the head of a pin. But what's so admirable about him is his marvelous contempt for the machinery of movies and even movies themselves - a kind of anarchistic,nihilistic contempt for the medium- which, when he's at his best and most vigorous, is very exciting."
This is amazing. Truly some great material here. Thank you!
> JLG
Compare to when he himself touched on sex with The Immortal Story and The Other Side of the Wind, which does have a more “romantic” approach to it. Likely the influence of Oja Kodar

Yes, I was thinking about these two in contrast to Citizen Kane or  Touch of Evil and ideas. I've never particularly thought of either films of ideas, where as Weekend, for example, gets me going down rabbit holes of ideas.
I really like the Otto Preminger takes. He was right imo.
They make philosophical claims or stances?
Yeah watch the movies lol
I didn’t like Breathless by Godard. Not sure why I should bother with two more by him. I don’t think films can do philosophy. Film and literature are two different species.
You wanna play blind man, go walk with the shepherd
Truth is easily spoke. But go ahead with your riddles.

Films can definitely do philosophy... You're not giving Godard a 2nd chance and if you don't want to, that's fine, but don't act like he doesn't have more to offer.

Literature is definitely different from movies, but movies can also do things literature can't
I really tried with Breathless but idk the characters weren’t giving me much.

Not everything works the same for everyone. You might enjoy more some of his other films.

I, too, have directors whose most famous film isn't the one I connected with the most.

I haven't seen much Godard either, but Contempt connected more with me.

Oh to be this good with words off the cuff. So eloquent.
